title: Skeletal Muscle: Length, Load and Speed

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: Why does an activated skeletal muscle do no external work both when it lifts nothing and when it holds a load equal to its isometric force?
cards.back: External work is force times the distance the load moves. Lifting nothing, there is no force; holding a load it cannot move, there is no distance. So power must peak at a load in between.
cards.quote: Lifting nothing, there is no force. Holding a load it cannot move, there is no distance.

cards.front: In the rule "length sets the ceiling, load sets the speed" for skeletal muscle, what is the ceiling (F0), and what sets it?
cards.back: F0 is the most force a fully activated muscle can hold at a given sarcomere length. Filament overlap at that length sets it.
cards.quote: At each sarcomere length, filament overlap fixes the most force a fully activated muscle can hold, F0.

cards.front: On the descending limb of the length-tension curve, why does active force fall as a sarcomere is stretched?
cards.back: Overlap is lost. On the plateau thin filaments reach every myosin head; stretched further, fewer heads face actin, so force falls in line with the lost overlap.
cards.quote: Stretch the sarcomere and fewer heads face actin, so force falls in line with the lost overlap.

cards.front: Why does active force also fall at short sarcomere lengths, left of the plateau of the frog length-tension curve?
cards.back: Filaments collide. Thin filaments cross into the opposite half-sarcomere and thick filaments meet the Z lines. The loss is usually read as interference, not too little overlap.
cards.quote: That loss is usually read as interference, with thin filaments crossing into the opposite half-sarcomere and thick filaments meeting the Z lines, not as too little overlap.

cards.front: Beyond the plateau, a resting skeletal muscle resists stretch. How is active tension obtained from a measured tension at a given length?
cards.back: Active tension = total tension minus passive tension (from titin and connective tissue) at the same length.
cards.quote: Active tension is total tension minus passive tension at the same length.

cards.front: Assume the descending limb of a fibre's length-tension curve is a straight line from full force at 2.20 µm to zero at 3.65 µm. What fraction of plateau force can the fibre hold at a sarcomere length of 2.80 µm?
cards.back: Limb length = 3.65 − 2.20 = 1.45 µm. Distance short of zero = 3.65 − 2.80 = 0.85 µm. Fraction = 0.85 / 1.45 = 0.586, about 59 percent of plateau force.
cards.quote: Assume the descending limb is a straight line from full force at 2.20 µm to zero at 3.65 µm.

cards.front: Extra filling stretches heart muscle, and a skeletal muscle fibre is stretched from its plateau onto the descending limb. Predict the change in active force in each.
cards.back: Heart muscle: force rises. Skeletal fibre: force falls.
cards.why: Heart muscle normally works below its optimal length, so stretch moves it toward the plateau. Beyond the plateau, stretch reduces filament overlap.
cards.quote: Heart muscle normally works below its optimal length, where stretch raises force

cards.front: Distinguish a concentric from an eccentric contraction of skeletal muscle.
cards.back: Concentric: the active muscle shortens. Eccentric: the active muscle is pulled longer because the load exceeds the force it is producing, as in the thigh muscles walking downhill.
cards.quote: Eccentric: the active muscle is pulled longer because the load exceeds the force it is producing, as the thigh muscles are when you walk downhill.

cards.front: A skeletal muscle contraction in which length is held is isometric; one with a constant load while length changes is {{c1::isotonic}}.
cards.quote: Isometric: length held (as above). Isotonic: constant load while length changes.

cards.front: In Hill's force-velocity experiment, tetanized frog sartorius at about 0 °C was released to lift a load on a lever. From the length-time trace, when and how is shortening speed read?
cards.back: From the steady slope just after the brief jerk at release, early, before shortening has changed the ceiling F0 much. One speed per load gives the force-velocity curve.
cards.quote: Read the speed early, just after the jerk, before the muscle has shortened enough to change its ceiling F0 much.

cards.front: In cross-bridge terms, why does a heavier load make an active skeletal muscle shorten more slowly?
cards.back: Fast sliding lets binding sites pass heads quickly, so fewer heads attach and some are dragged past their pulling point. A heavy load slows sliding until enough heads attach to bear it.
cards.quote: The muscle shortens at the speed at which just enough heads are attached to carry the load.

cards.front: Is the force-velocity curve of shortening skeletal muscle a straight line from vmax to F0? Describe its shape.
cards.back: No. It sags (Hill's points lie on a rectangular hyperbola, a fit; real fibres depart at extreme loads): speed falls steeply with the first bit of load, then more gently to zero at F0. In the model muscle, half of F0 gives only one-sixth of vmax.
cards.why: A straight line is what a stretched spring slowed by a viscous brake would give, so the sag was evidence against that picture.
cards.quote: It sags: speed falls steeply with the first bit of load, then more gently until it reaches zero at F0

cards.front: A model muscle has F0 = 100 N, vmax = 0.40 m/s and a/F0 = 0.25. Using Hill's equation in the form v = b (F0 − F) / (F + a), with b = vmax × a/F0, find its shortening speed and external power against a 20 N load.
cards.quote: A model muscle: F0 = 100 N, vmax = 0.40 m/s, a/F0 = 0.25.

cards.front: For a shortening muscle with the usual force-velocity curvature (a/F0 near 0.25), at what load and speed does external power peak?
cards.back: At about a third of F0 (0.31 F0), moving at about a third of vmax.
cards.quote: power peaks near a load of 31 N, about a third of F0, where the muscle moves at about a third of its top speed
cards.section: Power peaks at a middle load

cards.front: Most people guess that a muscle's power peaks at half of F0. Why is the best load lower?
cards.back: Half of F0 would be right for a straight force-velocity line. On the sagging curve, speed has already fallen far by half of F0, so the best load comes earlier.
cards.quote: Half of F0 would be right for a straight line, but on the sagging curve speed has already fallen far by then, so the best load comes earlier.
cards.section: Power peaks at a middle load

cards.front: A muscle has F0 = 60 N, vmax = 0.50 m/s and a/F0 = 0.25, so its best load is 0.309 of F0 and it moves that load at 0.309 of vmax. What is its peak external power?
cards.section: Power peaks at a middle load

cards.front: In the Hill model muscle (peak 3.82 W on the plateau), stretching to 3.00 µm leaves F0 at 0.448 of its plateau value. Assume vmax and a/F0 are unchanged. Predict peak power and the speed at which it occurs.
cards.back: Peak power falls by the same factor, to 0.448 × 3.82 = 1.71 W; the best speed (0.1236 m/s) does not move. The best load falls to 13.85 N.
cards.why: Combines the length-tension ceiling with the power rule: the best load is a fixed fraction of F0 and moves at a fixed fraction of vmax. A model exercise only, not a frog prediction.
cards.quote: The ceiling fell, peak power fell by the same factor, and the best speed did not move.
cards.section: Power peaks at a middle load

cards.front: A skeletal muscle holds a load isometrically. It does no external work. Does it still consume ATP?
cards.back: Yes. It keeps splitting ATP. The power curve describes external power, not ATP use.
cards.quote: This is external power: an isometric muscle does no external work, yet it keeps splitting ATP.
cards.section: Power peaks at a middle load

cards.front: A {{c1::twitch}} is the mechanical response of a muscle fibre to a single action potential.
cards.quote: A twitch is the mechanical response to a single action potential.
cards.section: Activation: how much of the ceiling you get

cards.front: Why does a single twitch fall short of a skeletal muscle's full force F0?
cards.back: One calcium release may not fill every troponin site, and activation is brief: calcium is pumped back before cross-bridges have stretched the series elastic parts (tendon, the heads) enough for force to build fully.
cards.quote: It falls short of F0 partly because one release may not fill every troponin site and partly because activation is brief.
cards.section: Activation: how much of the ceiling you get

cards.front: Why does a second action potential, arriving before a skeletal fibre has relaxed, produce more force than one alone (summation)?
cards.back: Its calcium adds to what the first left behind: cytosolic calcium rises further and stays high longer, more troponin stays occupied, and force has time to climb higher.
cards.quote: If a second action potential arrives before relaxation is complete, its calcium adds to what the first left behind
cards.section: Activation: how much of the ceiling you get

cards.front: How does the force record of an unfused tetanus differ from that of a fused tetanus?
cards.back: Unfused (moderate stimulation rates): force shows ripples. Fused (higher rates): force is smooth and approaches the ceiling F0.
cards.quote: At moderate rates the force record shows ripples, an unfused tetanus.
cards.section: Activation: how much of the ceiling you get

cards.front: Name the three main human skeletal muscle fibre types and their metabolic labels.
cards.back: Type I: slow oxidative. Type IIA: fast oxidative-glycolytic. Type IIX: fast glycolytic.
cards.quote: type I (slow oxidative), type IIA (fast oxidative-glycolytic) and type IIX (fast glycolytic).
cards.section: Fibre types set the top speed

cards.front: What makes human type I muscle fibres red and fatigue resistant?
cards.back: Myoglobin (oxygen transport) and dense capillaries make them red; abundant mitochondria support oxidative metabolism and fatigue resistance.
cards.quote: They are red from myoglobin (oxygen transport) and dense capillaries, rich in mitochondria, and resistant to fatigue.
cards.section: Fibre types set the top speed

cards.front: Does skeletal muscle fibre type mainly change F0 or vmax, and why?
cards.back: Mainly vmax. Speed follows the rate of the myosin ATPase and cross-bridge cycle, whereas force per cross-sectional area differs much less between types.
cards.quote: Force per cross-sectional area differs much less between types than speed does. So fibre type mainly moves vmax, not the ceiling.
cards.section: Fibre types set the top speed

cards.front: A motor unit of type I fibres and one of type IIX fibres are driven at the same moderate firing rate. Which is more likely to give a smooth, fused tetanus, and why?
cards.back: The type I unit.
cards.why: Type I fibres twitch more slowly, so successive twitches overlap more and fuse at lower firing rates.
cards.quote: Type I fibres twitch more slowly, so their twitches fuse at lower firing rates.
cards.section: Fibre types set the top speed

cards.front: A type IIX fibre and a type I fibre have the same F0 and the same force-velocity curvature, but the IIX fibre's vmax is three times higher. Compare their peak power and the load at which each peaks.
cards.back: The IIX fibre gives three times the peak power, at the same fraction of F0 (so the same best load).
cards.why: At fixed curvature peak power scales with F0 × vmax; the IIX fibre moves the same best load three times faster.
cards.quote: At fixed curvature peak power scales with F0 × vmax: the best load is the same fraction of F0 for both
cards.section: Fibre types set the top speed

cards.front: In muscle, PCr + ADP + H+ → creatine + ATP is catalysed by {{c1::creatine kinase}}.
cards.back: Phosphocreatine is the first buffer of ATP, at several times the ATP concentration in resting human muscle.
cards.quote: PCr + ADP + H+ → creatine + ATP (creatine kinase)
cards.section: Three ATP supplies, running at once

cards.front: During a burst of contraction, phosphocreatine breakdown regenerates ATP. Considered alone, what does this reaction do to intracellular pH, and why?
cards.back: It tends to raise pH (make the cytosol slightly more alkaline).
cards.why: The creatine kinase reaction (PCr + ADP + H+ → creatine + ATP) consumes a proton.
cards.quote: The reaction consumes a proton, which matters below.
cards.section: Three ATP supplies, running at once

cards.front: Why do fixed "10-second" and "2-minute" windows misdescribe the ATP supplies of working muscle?
cards.back: Phosphocreatine, glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation all run at the same time, with shares that shift with exercise intensity and duration.
cards.quote: All three run together, with shares that shift with intensity and duration, so fixed "10-second" or "2-minute" windows misdescribe them.
cards.section: Three ATP supplies, running at once

cards.front: In rats exercised to exhaustion, lactate was removed within 15 minutes, while oxygen uptake stayed above rest for 120 minutes. What does this show about post-exercise oxygen uptake?
cards.back: The extra oxygen is not simply repayment for lactate (the old oxygen debt). It is now called EPOC, with several sources: phosphocreatine resynthesis and refilling oxygen stores early, raised temperature and hormones later.
cards.quote: In rats exercised to exhaustion, Brooks and Gaesser (1980) found lactate removed within 15 minutes, while oxygen uptake stayed above rest for 120 minutes.
cards.section: Three ATP supplies, running at once

cards.front: {{c1::Fatigue}} is a fall in force or power during repeated activity that recovers with rest.
cards.quote: Fatigue is a fall in force or power during repeated activity that recovers with rest.

cards.front: In terms of F0, vmax and curvature, why can a fatigued muscle's power fall further than its isometric force?
cards.back: Fatigue usually lowers F0, often lowers vmax, and in most studies makes the force-velocity curve sag more. Power depends on all three.
cards.quote: Power depends on all three, so it can fall further than isometric force.

cards.front: In a fatigued model muscle, F0 falls by 25 percent and vmax by 20 percent, with force-velocity curvature unchanged. By what percentage does peak power fall?
cards.back: Peak power scales with F0 × vmax: 0.75 × 0.80 = 0.60, a 40 percent fall.
cards.quote: As an illustration in the model muscle, a 20 percent fall in F0 cuts peak power by 20 percent

cards.front: In a model muscle, fatigue lowers F0 and vmax by 20 percent each and lowers a/F0 from 0.25 to 0.15. Peak power as a fraction of F0 × vmax equals f², where f = 0.309 at a/F0 = 0.25 and 0.265 at 0.15. Find the total fall in peak power and the share due to extra sag.
cards.back: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64 (a 36 percent fall). Sag adds a factor of 0.265² / 0.309² = 0.74. Total 0.64 × 0.74 = 0.47, a fall of about 53 percent.
cards.why: Rests on peak power scaling with F0 × vmax and on a sharper sag lowering the best-load fraction.
cards.quote: let a/F0 drop from 0.25 to 0.15 as well and the peak shrinks from 0.309² to 0.265² of F0 × vmax

cards.front: If not the lactate ion, what are the leading candidate causes of force loss in skeletal muscle fatigue?
cards.back: Inorganic phosphate (acting on cross-bridges and on calcium release), failure of calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and ionic changes that affect the action potential.
cards.why: Protons contribute too, but to a smaller degree near body temperature.
cards.quote: Leading alternatives are inorganic phosphate (Pi), which acts on cross-bridges and on calcium release, failure of calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

cards.front: Why might experiments on cold muscle preparations have overstated the role of acid in fatigue? Cite the experiment on intact mouse fibres.
cards.back: Acidifying single mouse fibres by about 0.5 pH unit with CO2 cut tetanic force 28 percent at 12 °C but only 10 percent at 32 °C, with no significant change in vmax at 32 °C. The cost near body temperature is smaller, though not zero.
cards.quote: Cold preparations overstate the effect of acidosis; the authors concluded that direct inhibition of force by acidification is not a major factor

cards.front: In a laser trap, a small group of purified chicken myosin heads pulls on one actin filament. Lowering pH from 7.4 to 6.5 cuts average peak force by about 20 percent; adding 15 mM phosphate at pH 6.5 largely abolishes high-force events and makes events brief. Interpret.
cards.back: Protons and phosphate both act directly on the motor, and the different patterns point to different steps; phosphate seems to make myosin let go of actin sooner.
cards.why: No membrane, sarcoplasmic reticulum or lactate is present, so the effects are on myosin itself.
cards.quote: At pH 6.5, adding 15 mM phosphate largely abolished the high-force events, and events became brief, suggesting that myosin let go of actin sooner.

cards.front: Purified myosin loses about 20 percent of its force at pH 6.5 in a laser trap, yet acidifying intact mouse fibres at 32 °C costs only 10 percent of tetanic force. Why do these results not conflict?
cards.back: The trap shows that protons can act on the motor, not how much they contribute in working muscle. Its conditions differ: chicken proteins, low ATP, a fixed buffer, no lactate. The intact-fibre result measures the cost near body temperature.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's stated limits of each preparation.
cards.quote: which does not show how much either contributes in working mammalian muscle at body temperature; the shares are still debated

cards.front: In living rats, twitch force during repeated stimulation is followed with phosphorus magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and force tracks phosphate more consistently than protons. Does this show that phosphate causes the force decline?
cards.back: No. It is an association, not a test of cause, though it fits phosphate as a leading candidate.
cards.quote: In living rats, twitch force tracked phosphate more consistently than protons, an association rather than a test of cause

cards.front: In McArdle disease, muscle glycogen phosphorylase is missing. During brief intense contractions, predict lactate, intracellular pH and force, and say what this implies about lactate as a cause of fatigue.
cards.back: Lactate barely rises; pH does not fall and may rise slightly; yet force fails early. So lactate accumulation cannot be a necessary cause of fatigue.
cards.why: Glycogen cannot feed glycolysis, so little lactate or acid is made, and creatine kinase consumes protons.
cards.quote: Fatigue here develops without acidosis or a rise in lactate, so lactate accumulation cannot be its necessary cause.

cards.front: After several minutes of moderate exercise, a person with McArdle disease (no muscle glycogen phosphorylase) often tolerates more work, the "second wind". Which fuel supply is it consistent with?
cards.back: Consistent with rising delivery of blood glucose and fatty acids to oxidative metabolism, which bypasses the blocked use of muscle glycogen.
cards.quote: After several minutes of moderate exercise, more work is often tolerated (the "second wind"), consistent with rising delivery of blood glucose and fatty acids to oxidative metabolism.

cards.front: Repeated all-out sprints are performed by a muscle rich in type IIX fibres and by one rich in type I fibres. Predict which loses power faster, and why power falls more than isometric force.
cards.back: The IIX-rich muscle: IIX fibres rely mostly on glycolysis and fatigue quickly, while type I fibres are mitochondria-rich and fatigue resistant. Fatigue lowers F0 and usually vmax, so power falls most.
cards.why: Combines fibre-type metabolism with the rule that power depends on F0, vmax and curvature.
cards.quote: IIX fibres rely mostly on glycolysis and fatigue quickly.
cards.section: Fibre types set the top speed

cards.front: How does the skeletal muscle pump aid venous return from the legs?
cards.back: Contracting calf muscles squeeze the deep veins; one-way valves let blood move only toward the heart; on relaxation the veins refill from below.
cards.quote: Contracting calf muscles squeeze the deep veins between them, and one-way valves let blood move only toward the heart

cards.front: A person stands motionless for a long time, then walks in place. Predict the change in venous return from the legs, and why.
cards.back: Venous return from the legs rises when walking.
cards.why: Rhythmic calf contraction squeezes the deep veins, and valves let blood move only toward the heart; standing still loses this muscle pump.
cards.quote: This muscle pump aids venous return from the legs (cardiac output and venous return).

cards.front: Why is shivering an effective way for skeletal muscle to make heat?
cards.back: It is involuntary, rhythmic contraction that does almost no external work, so nearly all its energy becomes heat. Even in cycling, at most about a quarter appears as external work.
cards.quote: Shivering is involuntary, rhythmic contraction that does almost no external work, so nearly all its energy becomes heat

cards.front: Design an experiment comparing the force-velocity and power curves of isolated mouse soleus (slower, type I and IIA) and EDL (mostly fast type II) muscles, and predict the result.
cards.back: At optimal length, record a reference tetanus (F0), then afterloaded releases to loads of about 5 to 90 percent of F0; read early steady speed; normalize force to cross-sectional area; fit Hill's equation; P = F × v. Predict similar force per area, higher vmax and higher peak power in EDL.
cards.why: Rests on fibre type moving vmax more than force per area. Controls: same temperature and stimulation, random load order, repeated reference tetanus.
cards.quote: Prediction: similar force per area but higher vmax in EDL, so its power curve peaks higher.
